title: Debugging Basics
summary: A bug is a place where what the program **does** differs from what you **expected**. Debugging is finding that place. Do it with a method: read the message, look at the values, narrow it down.
markdown:
## Bugs are normal Every programmer writes bugs all day. What separates a beginner from an expert is not how few bugs they write. It is how quickly they find them. That is a skill, and it has a method. ```mermaid flowchart LR A["Something is wrong"] --> B["Make it happen
again on demand"] B --> C["Narrow down
where"] C --> D["Understand
why"] D --> E["Fix it"] E --> F["Test again"] F -->|"still wrong"| C ``` The step people skip is the fourth. If you change things until it seems to work without knowing why, the bug is usually still there. ## First, which kind of problem is it? | What you see | Kind | Where to look | |---|---|---| | It will not build | Compile or linker error | The **Problems** tab. Start with the first message. | | It builds, then stops with an error | Crash | The message in the console, and the last thing printed before it | | It runs and gives the wrong answer | Logic error | The values of your variables, step by step | ## Reading a compiler message ``` main.cpp(8,5): error C2146: missing ';' before identifier 'std' │ │ │ └── what the compiler got stuck on │ │ └── column │ └── line └── file ``` Go to that line. If it looks fine, look at the line **above** it. A missing `;` is only noticed when the compiler reaches the next thing. ## Technique 1: print the values When the answer is wrong, some variable holds a value you did not expect. So look. ```cpp #include int main() { int price{ 4 }; int quantity{ 3 }; int total{ price + quantity }; std::cerr << "DEBUG total=" << total << '\n'; std::cout << "You owe " << total << '\n'; return 0; } ``` `std::cerr` works like `std::cout`. It is meant for messages to the programmer, not for the program's real output. The `DEBUG` label makes these lines easy to spot and delete when you have finished. Here the debug line shows `total=7`. You expected 12, so the mistake is on the line that calculates `total`. ## Technique 2: be the computer Go through the program one line at a time and write down what every variable holds. This is called **tracing**, and it is the most reliable debugging tool there is. ```cpp int a{ 4 }; int b{ 5 }; int c{ 6 }; int average{ a + b + c / 3 }; ``` | After the line | a | b | c | average | |---|---|---|---|---| | `int a{ 4 };` | 4 | | | | | `int b{ 5 };` | 4 | 5 | | | | `int c{ 6 };` | 4 | 5 | 6 | | | `int average{ ... };` | 4 | 5 | 6 | 4 + 5 + (6 / 3) = **11** | The trace shows the problem. Division happens before addition, so only `c` is divided. The fix is brackets: `(a + b + c) / 3`. > [!tip] Do what the code says, not what you meant > The difficult part of tracing is being honest. Your eyes see what you intended to write. Follow each symbol exactly as it is written. ## Technique 3: cut the problem in half When you have no idea where the mistake is, print a value in the **middle** of the program. ```mermaid flowchart TD S["Print a value halfway through"] --> Q{"Is it what
you expected?"} Q -->|"yes"| L["The mistake is in
the second half"] Q -->|"no"| E["The mistake is in
the first half"] L --> R["Repeat on that half"] E --> R ``` Each check halves the search. Even in a thousand lines you find the spot in about ten checks. ## Technique 4: explain it out loud Describe your code line by line to someone else, or to an object on your desk. Programmers call this *rubber duck debugging*. You will often stop mid-sentence because you have just heard yourself say something that is not true. ## Writing fewer bugs | Habit | Why it helps | |---|---| | Run after every few lines | A new problem must be in the lines you just wrote | | Read every warning | A warning usually means "this is legal, and probably not what you meant" | | Give every variable a starting value | Removes a whole family of unpredictable behaviour | | Keep functions small | A small piece is easy to check on its own | ## Later: a debugger Professional tools such as Visual Studio include a **debugger**. It pauses a running program on any line you choose, shows every variable, and lets you move forward one line at a time. It automates the tracing you just did by hand. Once you know how to trace, a debugger takes minutes to learn. ## Check yourself ```quiz ? A program builds and runs but gives the wrong answer. What kind of error is it, and what do you do? - A compile error; read the first compiler message - A linker error; check that every function has a definition + A logic error; check the variables' values until you find the first one that is wrong - A logic error; rewrite the program from scratch > It built and ran, so it is a **logic error**. Print the values or trace by hand until you find the first one that is not what you expected. ? The compiler reports an error on a line that looks correct. Where do you look next? + The line above it - The last line of the file - The first line of the file - The line below it > A missing `;` or bracket is reported where the compiler notices it, which is often one line after the real mistake. ? Why print a value in the middle of the program first? - Because printing slows the program down, which reveals the bug - Because the middle of a program is where bugs usually are + It tells you which half the mistake is in, so each check halves the search - Because the compiler only checks the middle of the program > Checking the middle tells you whether the mistake is before or after that point. Each check cuts the search area in half. ? What is tracing? - Letting the compiler list every line it compiled + Going through the code line by line, noting what each variable holds after each line - Printing every variable once at the end of the program - Copying the program into a new file to see if it still fails > Tracing is "being the computer": you follow each line in order and write down every variable's value as it changes. ```
ideas:
1. The averaging code above prints 11. Fix it and confirm the answer is 5.
2. Trace this by hand before running it: `int x{ 10 }; x = x / 4; x = x * 4;`. What does `x` hold?
3. Break a working program of yours in a small way, wait a minute, then find the problem using only printed values.

cards.q: A program builds and runs but gives the wrong answer. What kind of error is it, and what do you do?
cards.a:
A logic error; check the variables' values until you find the first one that is wrong

It built and ran, so it is a **logic error**. Print the values or trace by hand until you find the first one that is not what you expected.

cards.q: The compiler reports an error on a line that looks correct. Where do you look next?
cards.a:
The line above it

A missing `;` or bracket is reported where the compiler notices it, which is often one line after the real mistake.

cards.q: Why print a value in the middle of the program first?
cards.a:
It tells you which half the mistake is in, so each check halves the search

Checking the middle tells you whether the mistake is before or after that point. Each check cuts the search area in half.

Going through the code line by line, noting what each variable holds after each line

Tracing is "being the computer": you follow each line in order and write down every variable's value as it changes.
